subtopic: TABLING OF INSTRUMENTS ADOPTED AT FIFTIETH CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: TABLING OF INSTRUMENTS ADOPTED AT FIFTIETH CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with article 19 of the constitution of the International Labour Organization, and with the permission of the house, I would like to table the text in English and French of instruments adopted at the 50th International Labour Conference held in Geneva in June, 1966. Four instruments were adopted at that conference-two conventions and two recommendations.
The I.L.O. constitution requires the government of a member state to bring conventions and recommendations adopted by the International Labour Conference "before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies for the enactment of legislation or other action." In the case of a federal state, the constitution further obliges the federal government to refer instruments which are deemed to be wholly or partially within provincial legislative competence to the appropriate provincial authorities "for the enactment of legislation or other action."
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), a copy of which I should like also to table with the consent of the house, is that the subject matter of each convention is within federal legislative jurisdiction, and that the subject matter of each of the recommendations is partially within federal legislative jurisdiction and partially within provincial legislative jurisdiction.
Convention 125 sets up minimum international standards for certificates of competency for officers on salt water fishing vessels. In Canada the standards in this convention have been studied by the departments concerned. The requirements for engineers I am pleased to say are being met in Canada.
Convention 126 deals with accommodation of crews on salt water fishing vessels. Here we have associated problems to discuss with the provinces concerned. This convention has been studied by the departments concerned in order to ascertain the extent to which it agrees with Canadian standards for such accommodation. I am pleased to say there has been substantial conformity in practice, but there are still a few problems to be overcome before ratification can be considered.
Recommendation 126 outlines vocational training programs for fishermen. Recommendation 127 concerns the role of co-operatives in developing countries. As hon. members no doubt are aware, the I.L.O. constitution obliges governments of federal states to arrange for periodic consultations between federal and provincial authorities with a view to promoting action to give effect to the provisions of international instruments adopted by the International Labour Conference. In addition to our regular consultations my department is continuing to consult with other federa authorities in respect of provincial areas of the I.L.O. conventions.
I should like to add that I was privileged to take part in a ceremony last fall at which my colleague the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) formally presented the instruments of ratification of two I.L.O. conventions on behalf of the government of Canada: Convention 45 concerning the employment of women on underground work in mines, and convention 122 concerning employment policy. I might say that that occasion was made more pleasurable by the fact that the eighth regional conference of American states members of the I.L.O. was meeting in Ottawa at that time.
With the permission of the house I should like to file the conventions and regulations.

The minister with his wide knowledge of the law, which is apparent in the statement he has just placed before the house, has underlined and emphasized the seriousness of the situation facing this nation in the field of international affairs in respect of those matters which may or may not fall within provincial jurisdiction.
Once more in centennial year I suggest that what he has said is further evidence of the need for this nation to convene a national constitutional conference to the end that we will determine once and for all the rights of this nation as a nation to enter into treaties, and also at the same time to assure that the infringement of impingement of treaty rights by particular provinces shall not be compromised.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Manpower and Immigration) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Immigration Act to increase from twelve million dollars to twenty million dollars the present limit on the total amount of outstanding advances at any one time that may be made to enable the
May 25. 1967

Minister of Manpower and Immigration to make loans to immigrants to assist them with the expenses of their transportation to Canada.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution introduces what must be one of the shortest items of legislation ever proposed in parliament. It seeks to amend one word in the Immigration Act, changing the word "twelve" to "twenty". The change is far from trivial, however, because the words following are "million dollars".
The proposal is to raise from $12 million to $20 million the ceiling on the amount of assisted passage loans to immigrants that may be outstanding at any one time. The change is necessary because of the relatively large numbers of immigrants who have been coming to Canada recently. The present ceiling would force us to cut down sharply the assistance we are able to give.
I think we agree, with little difficulty, that such action would be undesirable and unfair. I hope therefore that we can proceed soon to consider the bill itself. We are dealing of course with a financial measure and a resolution is necessary. The bill itself is so short and simple that I hope, if the house agrees, I might make my detailed explanation when we come to second reading. I hope the house will give unanimous consent that we go immediately to second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext: Probably, Mr. Chairman. [English]

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, normally we would wish to accommodate the minister in his suggestion. When such suggestions are normally made they are preceded by consultations across the floor of the house. Such consultations to the best of my knowledge have not taken place, and there are questions which the minister ought to answer before we proceed to second reading of the bill.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
If the bill is as simple as the minister has indicated I would have no objection to seeing it read the second time and given final approval today. But I think the proper time to make a full and elaborate statement as to its purpose is now, on the resolution stage. If we accept the minister's statement at its face value, then the bill amounts to nothing more than a simple piece of financial window dressing, in which case it will come as a great disappointment to the house. We on this side were hoping that the resolution would accomplish something more than appears on the face of it-that it would mark a new approach to immigration policy as far as assistance to immigrants is concerned, rather than a continuation of the piecemeal, patchwork programs of the past.
I think the time has come to adopt imaginative and dynamic new policies in relation to the assistance of immigrants. All that is proposed here is that the amount of money available in the revolving fund should be increased. This is of course important; it shows we are making progress. But there has been no change in principle-no real improvement.
The minister should have given us an introductory statement, making it clear that the government intends to follow a dynamic immigration policy and is not merely coasting along. This proposal merely to increase the number of dollars available is less than satisfactory, for a number of reasons. In the first place, it seems to offer less than the fulfilment of the government's own proposals as set out in the white paper. At page 38 of that document, after a discussion of the assisted passage scheme which is authorized by section 69 of the Immigration Act, we find these words:
However, the scheme needs revision to reflect the universal and non-discriminatory selection policy outlined in this white paper. Therefore, subject to parliamentary approval of the necessary funds, it is proposed that loans be made available on a universal basis to qualified unsponsored immigrants, including their wives and minor dependant children, up to a maximum of $1,500 for a family unit.

May 25, 1967
Immigration Act
When the minister tells us that all we need do is increase the amount, he is not even carrying out the policy enunciated in the white paper itself. As well as I can recall, the assisted passage scheme has been confined exclusively in the past to Europe, and indeed it does not extend to all parts of Europe; it is inapplicable in Yugoslavia or Soviet bloc countries, for the simple reason that unsponsored immigrants are not normally accepted from those countries. The Netherlands and Norway-in other days, at least, and probably now-object to the operation of the scheme within their borders. I believe also that the scheme does not operate in Malta, in Spain or in the Azores. Today we are being asked to accept a change from $12 million to $20 million blindly, in the absence of any indication of what is planned or whether there will be any change in basic policy.
I suggest that the committee must decide whether a loan scheme is sufficient or whether a system of subsidy should be coupled with it. The white paper rejects out of hand the use of migrant subsidies as a promotional device. I am far from certain that this is the correct attitude. Australia has had a most satisfactory experience with a system of subsidization. I have in hand a pamphlet which describes the Australian system. Under this scheme the fare, door to door, from the British Isles to Australia is only ten pounds sterling. Young people under 19 travel free. This means that a husband and wife with any number of children under 19 can go to Australia at a total cost in fares of only twenty pounds sterling or about sixty dollars Canadian. Those who travel under this assisted passage scheme use the normal passenger shipping services or air lines. Their payment of ten pounds toward the cost is simply the result of an arrangement between themselves and the government of Australia; as far as the shipping or air line companies are concerned, passengers have the same status and accommodation as anyone who has paid the full economy class fare.
There can be no doubt that Australia has been much more successful than Canada has been in the promotion of immigration from the British Isles. In most years their intake has exceeded ours by two to one. This should not, and need not, be the case. In my view this country has attractions unequalled by those of our great sister land. But it is a fact that the promotion of immigration by Australia has been much more consistent and much more vigorous than ours. I believe the government and the special joint committee

of the Senate and the House of Commons should examine Australia's promotional efforts with a view to emulating them. For the present, we simply cannot compete in the British Isles with the financial allurements offered by Australia. As competition for desirable immigrants grows, I feel we may become increasingly shut out of the British Isles unless we adopt new and more vigorous policies.
The weakness of this resolution is that it deals only with assisted passages-with transportation costs. But the period during which a new immigrant may well require most assistance is during the first weeks, or months, of his settlement in Canada. Yet there is not a word in this resolution about settlement arrangements-about educational facilities, language instruction, facilities for personal guidance or advice to immigrants after their arrival here.
A basic weakness of the department for years has been a too great concentration of interest on the landing of immigrants in Canada, leaving resultant problems to the provinces and the municipalities. My feeling is that this is not good enough and that a major expansion of the settlement, education and welfare programs of the Department of Manpower and Immigration is essential. The very minimum requirement is genuine coordination with provincial and municipal programs. It is not enough to pay travel expenses and then leave the immigrant on his own, without counseling, without guidance, without language instruction, and dependant solely upon local services which, to say the least, are of diverse quality from community to community. When the government is seeking money to pay travel expenses for immigrants, the least it owes the House of Commons is to tell hon. members whether it has any plans at all to expand the services available to these newly-arrived persons.
Another failure, I suggest-

speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member refuses to give unanimous consent? I just want to know.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
The minister is quite right. I intend to make a speech on this resolution, and as far as I am concerned the resolution may then pass and I am prepared to deal with the bill this afternoon. But if the minister expects any co-operation from this side of the house, he knows perfectly well that I usually act as critic on immigration matters, and I am as near as the nearest
May 25, 1967

telephone. All he has to do is telephone me, not attempt to pull some stunt on the floor of the House of Commons.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
May I mention to the hon.
member that yesterday the acting house leader indicated that the bill we are dealing with would be called today. About a month ago I spoke to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and told him-unfortunately the hon. member for Carleton was not here at the time-that this fund would run out of money during May. He said he would be ready to co-operate during the new session, even during the debate in reply to the speech from the throne.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
The minister will get his resolution through faster if he is prepared to be co-operative. I intend to make my statements in respect of what I believe are the deficiencies in this resolution, and I expect the minister to answer them. So far as I am concerned I am prepared to go ahead and deal with the second reading of the bill and, if necessary, put it through all stages this afternoon. But I venture to suggest that the minister, if he wants to get business through this house, knows perfectly well to whom he should come and discuss immigration matters, at least so far as the official opposition is concerned. He has enough experience already to know that.
I believe another deficiency of this resolution is that it deals not at all with the integration of the assisted passage proposals with the plans formulated by at least some of the provinces. For example, in May, 1966, the government of Manitoba embarked upon a new free passage program to attract immigrants to that province. What discussions have there been between the federal department and the government of Manitoba? How has the Manitoba scheme been working? How will it fit in with the proposals to follow this resolution? Have any of the other provinces adopted such plans or are they discussing them with the department of immigration? What are the Quebec proposals? What are the results of Premier Johnson's discussions in Paris? I believe the committee is entitled to know the answers to these questions before the resolution passes.
Another matter which I suggest is not at all clear from the resolution is whether transportation costs will be available to former Canadian citizens and their dependants established abroad who seek now to resettle in
Immigration Act
Canada. I believe this to be a very fruitful field and that travel costs should clearly be available to such persons.
The repatriation of Canadians now abroad is an important factor which should not be airily dismissed. Personally I was gratified that the government has adopted the basic principles of the report of Dr. E. F. Sheffield and Miss Mary Margot McGrail on the retrieval of Canadian graduate students from abroad. That report can be a significant contribution to future Canadian intellectual development.
The house, Mr. Chairman, knows that I am an unregenerate expansionist in immigration policy. Canada simply cannot achieve her manifest destiny without an increase in population much greater than can be achieved by natural growth. We need as well the cultural advantages of the best immigrants from other lands, and we need the continuing stimulus to our economy which expanded immigration brings.
I was disturbed to hear a senior member of the New Democratic party advocating in the house earlier this week a tap-off immigration policy because there is unemployment in some trades. That, sir, is totally contrary to my thinking and my beliefs. A tap-on, tap-off approach to immigration is self-defeating. I believe in immigration as a stimulus, not a depressant, to the economy, and a proper, consistent policy of immigrant selection will create additional jobs for Canadians rather than deprive Canadians of jobs.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
I do not want to be involved in a chicken and egg argument, but it is demonstrable that our periods of highest immigration intake have been our periods of maximum prosperity and national progress. Which comes first and which comes second, I care not. I believe they go hand in hand, and I hope the minister will pay no attention to the policy of the N.D.P. member of turning the tap off at the slightest sign of economic disturbance. My view is that we must set definite national objectives and then refuse to be deflected from them by every stray wind in the economic atmosphere.
We are prepared to support this resolution, but it simply does not begin to deal with the problem. It is just playing around with the fringes of what is a basic problem. I hope that the minister who has had perhaps the best press and public relations build up, of all

May 25, 1967
Immigration Act
the cabinet, unequalled by any previous minister oi immigration, will seek to establish entitlement to the accolades. If the mountainous labours on immigration produce mice of the vintage now under discussion in this committee I say that disillusionment is inevitable and retribution sure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are dealing here with a resolution preparatory to a bill which I understand is to be of a very narrow nature, increasing the amount of money available to the department for loans for assisted passage from $12 million to $20 million. On an earlier occasion when I followed the hon. member for Carleton in discussing the question of immigration I said that whenever I listened to the hon. member speak on immigration it seemed to me that what he was saying was, "Do as I say, not as I did," because to my knowledge this country never had so few immigrants as when the hon. member for Carleton was the minister for citizenship and immigration. I do not blame him. It happens that at that time the country did have large scale unemployment, and any minister in charge of immigration and any government would take that into consideration when setting out objectives.
Before continuing I wish to say I do not know which member of the New Democratic party the hon. member for Carleton referred to when he said that a senior N.D.P. member of parliament had urged turning off the tap on immigration. If there was such a member,
I want to say he was speaking only for himself and did not speak for our party. Our party has supported and will continue to support increased immigration. We recognize the fact that there are some problems. We recognize that when there is large scale unemployment that is something which has to be given consideration, but we believe and have constantly said for a long number of years that Canada needs more people and that immigration on a large scale is necessary. That is the policy of our party. We have expressed it previously, and I express it once more on behalf of our party.
We in the N.D.P. will support this resolution and the bill which will follow it. If we are going to have 25 per cent, 30 per cent or 35 per cent more immigration than we have had in recent years, which seems to be the level of increase to date this year, then naturally we shall have to provide more money for assisted passages.
I am not certain that I agree entirely with the hon. member for Carleton who thinks the 
time has come for us to wipe out the program of loans for assisted passages and replace it by a system of grants covering passage and other expenses of new immigrants. However, if we are to continue having much larger immigration from countries in southern Europe and from countries behind the iron curtain, involving people who are less affluent than those who come from Great Britain and other countries of northern and western Europe, it may be that we will have to assist them both with passage expenses and expenses of their establishment in Canada. This is a question which the department should keep under constant study. The department should not have fixed views on it, and I would hope that the standing committee which deals with immigration would look at this question when it meets again and examine our record in comparison with Australia to see whether we ought to change our policy. It is something worth considering.
I share the feelings of the hon. member for Carleton in expressing disappointment that this resolution and the bill to follow it deal with such a narrow part of the immigration question, particularly in the light of the white paper which promised such basic changes in our immigration policy and in the light of the statement made by the minister to the special joint committee which studied the white paper when he promised even more changes than those enunciated in the white paper and further expansion in the program of immigration.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I am not critical of the minister. The minister gave us a very brief and reasonable explanation of what will be contained in the bill. There is, however, nothing in what the minister said nor in what will be contained in the bill to indicate how far the government intends to go or how quickly it intends to proceed with the principles enunciated in the white paper and the principles which the minister has been enunciating in the speeches he has made all across the country. I join with the hon. member for Carleton and many others who have tried to indicate to the government that along with large scale immigration, which all of us support, tremendous problems will arise and in fact have arisen. The hon. member for Carleton raised in the house-this has been mentioned by myself and other members-the question of the tremendous problem which this country has to face when we have large scale immigration from countries in which the native tongue is
May 25, 1967

neither English nor French. We have had and will continue to have large scale immigration from countries such as Italy, Greece, Portugal and Spain. I am all for this. It seems to me, however, that when the federal government encourages this kind of immigration it ought to face up to the fact that it is creating tremendous problems for the cities and provinces to which these immigrants come, eventually for the federal government, and indeed for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who wears two hats.
There has been sufficient research and study for us to know that in cities like Toronto and Montreal the children of immigrants who come from the countries I have mentioned, for example, Italy, are not continuing their schooling. They are not finishing high school even though in cities such as Toronto the educational system is geared in such a way that it encourages them to attend high school. The drop-out rate is tremendous. I am told that the city of Toronto is spending in the neighbourhood of $1,500,000 a year in the field of education to try to encourage these people to remain in school and to learn English so they will be in a position to fit into society.
The Minister of Justice is here. He might well interrupt me as he interrupted my colleague from Danforth the other day when he was discussing the question of housing. I know that under our constitution the question of education is a provincial responsibility. The fact is, however, that these people who can speak neither English nor French are coming to Canada. I support the idea of their coming here. They come here with the encouragement of the federal government.
Unless we can encourage these people to learn English or French so they will be able to integrate into our society and unless we begin to co-operate with the provinces and help to finance the provincial programs so this can be done, the result of our failure to do so will show up a few years from now. At that time the minister in his capacity as minister of manpower will have the problem of trying to find jobs for people who to a large extent will be unemployable simply because they do not know the languages and the other techniques which are necessary in our society in order to find and hold a job. It seems to me that the minister and his department must face up to this problem now and not later.
There is one other problem which I think must be faced by the department. I greet with approval the statement of the minister-and 1 am sure this is spelled out in the legislation
Immigration Act
-that from now on the immigration policy of the government will be one in which there will be no vestige of the past discriminations that have been apparent with regard to race, colour and creed. I believe that more than the passage of legislation will be required in order to bring this into effect. In the past we have had not one but many illustrations of cases where officers of the department in the field have made very plain, from the type of questions which have been asked of immigrants and from the treatment prospective immigrants have received, that they do hold discriminatory views. In adopting these new policies it seems to me it is the responsibility of the department to make sure that the people who make the decisions know what is the policy of the department and the government so that discrimination on the basis of race, colour or creed will in fact disappear.
I should like to mention from memory a case which we had recently in the city of Winnipeg concerning an immigrant from the West Indies. This person was ordered to leave the country. He appealed his case. The appeal was refused by the department and he went to the court. The chief justice of the appeal court was scathing in his condemnation of the handling of the case by the department. The department furnished me with a copy of the proceedings of the appeal board. The questions were of a nature which indicated clearly that the officer in charge certainly had discriminatory views. The man was asked whether he was married. He replied that he was not. Then he was asked whether he had any children. I suggest to the minister that no officer of the department would ask that question of a white would-be immigrant. The only reason that question would be asked would be because of the prejudiced view of the departmental officer that somebody who is non-white would have lower morals than anyone else. I suggest that as soon as the legislation arising out of the white paper is enacted the minister and his department should adopt a crash program to educate the departmental officers. I would hate to see the same type of difficulty arise in respect of this department as arose in respect of the manpower offices and which was recently brought to the attention of the minister and his department.
I shall close by saying that if this resolution is merely a simple bill to increase the amount of money in the fund to $20 million in order to assist immigrants with the expenses of their transportation, we in this party will

May 25, 1987
Immigration Act
co-operate with the government. I do not think we will interfere with the passage of this bill through all stages today. I would hope, however, that at a very early date the minister would find some opportunity to inform the house and the country concerning the kind of legislation he intends to bring in to implement the very fine principles which the minister has been enunciating from one end of the country to the other. I should like to see some action on the speeches the minister has been making.
[DOT] (3:50 p.ra.)

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR TRANSPORTATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to comment on this resolution this afternoon I might point out that I have no objection to increasing the amount of the revolving fund available to would-be immigrants to this country, but in view of paragraph 34 of the white paper on immigration I feel I must speak in a definite way.
The House of Commons is given little if any opportunity to make comments in respect of the continual demands from one section of this country for better treatment than any other portion. When the announcement was made that certain radio stations were being converted to 100 per cent French usage and efforts were made to introduce the matter in the House of Commons we were told quite blandly by members of the cabinet that this matter had nothing to do with parliament but was a matter for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Board of Broadcast Governors. All we have to do is foot the bill to the tune of about $143 million this year.
When arrangements were made to provide bonuses for bilingual people as compared with unilingual people an effort was made to discuss it on the floor of the house and we were told then that this was a civil service commission matter which had nothing to do with parliament. We now have before us a resolution to increase from $12 million to $20 million the revolving fund to assist immigrants with the expenses of their transportation to Canada, and I relate the resolution directly to paragraph 34 of the white paper on immigration.
I have a copy of the white paper in my hand as well as four statements by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in respect of the white paper. May I preface my remarks by pointing out that the term "white paper" is a colloquial term for a government statement of policy. This definition is taken from page 659 of the Encyclopedia of Parliament by Norman Wilding and Philip
[Mr. Orlikow. j
Laundy. Mr. Laundy, by the way, is now a senior officer of the parliamentary library, having been engaged previously in similar work in Southern Rhodesia. He writes that "white paper" is a colloquial term for a government statement of policy, and I should like to emphasize the adjective "colloquial" because there are people in this country who might tell you that a white paper is something that can never be criticized, as if it almost came down with the tablets from the top of Mount Sinai.
I happen to be on the immigration study group of the Liberal party and I attended a number of meetings with the deputy minister and on occasion the present minister to discuss matters of immigration of importance to this nation. I was present in the minister's office with a group of Liberal members the night before the white paper came out. The deputy minister was there as well as senior officials of the department, and a very healthy discussion took place in the minister's office at his invitation.
A number of things were said and a number of things transpired that were for the good of Canada, but I will never forget that when one member of parliament asked why we could not look at the white paper that night before it was issued the next day there was absolute holy horror on the part of some at the thought that a member of parliament on the government side of the house should ask to see the white paper before it was introduced. Every member of the Liberal party is supposed to vote 100 per cent for the white paper or be called a rebel, a disturber or a person who does not co-operate with the government. What this really means is the cabinet. I never saw the Canadian immigration policy or white paper until every other member of parliament was given a copy last October, and I have been waiting since for an opportunity to speak about paragraph 34.
Let me also preface my remarks by reference to a statement in that book regarding the C.B.C. to which frequent reference has been made, "Nation and Province" by Professor J. C. Ricker and Professor J. T. Say-well. At page 43 the following statement appears:
So important is the cabinet that many people use the words cabinet and government as though they were synonymous.
I am sorry to say that members of the cabinet also use the words government and cabinet as though they were synonymous. As a result a private member, so-called, is given no opportunity to discuss many matters and
May 25, 1967



he does so at the risk of being called a disturber, a rebel, a hermit or a heretic. Private members are never asked about or told anything in advance.
In this regard let me refer hon. members to the remarks of the hon. member for Keno-ra-Rainy River of last October 31 during the debate on interim supply. They can be found in Hansard for last year at pages 9342 and 9343. At that time he pointed out that private members are asked nothing but are supposed to support measures laid before them without prior notice. The hon. member for Carleton need not think he is standing alone in not being advised of what is to be placed on the floor of the House of Commons. He is only one of a host of members including those on the so-called government side who are not told what is coming before the house.
In reference to paragraph 34 of the white paper let me point out that I speak only for the 70 per cent of the people of this country who are not French speaking, and no doubt I will be called a rabblerouser for speaking in this way. I have in my hand a copy of the March 20, 1967, issue of the Ottawa Journal. Under a two-column heading "Chretien Tells Rally", and, "French Must O.K. Cabinet Moves", we find the following statement:
Jean Chretien, parliamentary secretary to finance minister Sharp, said during the week end that French Canadian members of the federal cabinet "are in a position of strength at Ottawa".
"Nothing can be done without the agreement of the French speaking ministers," Mr. Chretien told a Liberal meeting here.
This article refers to a statement he made at Lachute. It is interesting to note that in Quebec French Canadian votes for the Liberal party during the last election, as shown in the returns by the chief electoral officer and in the Parliamentary Guide, numbered 742,824. The Liberals did not even receive half of the votes in the province of Quebec. The Liberals are in a minority position in Quebec, but according to Mr. Chretien nothing can be done without the agreement of the French speaking ministers. If the English were to say that nothing could be done without the agreement of the English speaking ministers, we would be called trouble-makers and told that there were minorities in the house which were being ignored. I am talking about majorities being ignored. The 742,824 French Liberal votes in Quebec represented 9.5 per cent of the total vote polled in Canada in the last election, but as the former parliamentary secretary said, nothing can be done
Immigration Act
without the agreement of the French speaking cabinet members.
I could go on at length in this regard but immigration is the matter before us. Requests are always being made by the French speaking section of this country for special treatment. The premier of Quebec has said that he will ignore the Supreme Court of Canada if it makes a ruling with regard to the pension rights of the provinces. We have all heard the statement that Labrador should be turned over to Quebec, that all the islands in Hudson Bay and Hudson Strait should be turned over to Quebec, and that the Indians and Eskimos in Quebec should be removed from the jurisdiction of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and placed under the jurisdiction of Quebec. I hope no one thinks that this is the end of the requests which will come from that one section of confederation. The Quebec federation of St. Jean Baptiste Societies is urging that all new Canadians not of British origin who enrol children in Quebec schools for the first time this fall be compelled to place them in French language schools.
The Globe and Mail of Wednesday, May 10, 1967, contained the following statement:
It would be dismaying to think of Quebec responding to these advances by adopting a policy of compulsory designation of schools to all newcomers-
Whence came this idea? It came from no other source than the Canadian government's white paper on immigration dated October, 1966, and issued by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. In paragraph 34 we read, for the first time in the history of Canada, that the Canadian government-the minister really means "cabinet", not "government" -that the present cabinet is anxious to change the age-long actions of immigrants to Canada settling west of the Ottawa river. This policy is set out in paragraph 34 of the white paper on immigration and reads as follows:
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
There is a broader consideration affecting the distribution of immigrants. While it has been spread more widely since the war than often in the past, it is still true to say that immigration effectively begins at the island of Montreal and goes west. The rate of immigration to areas east of the Ottawa river is generally low. Thus, disproportionately little of our immigration increases our French speaking population. This is largely because France, for many years now, has felt for itself a problem of relatively declining population and therefore has been much more discouraging of emigration than a country such as Britain. However, it also appears that some potential immigrants have felt

May 25, 1967
Immigration Act
that Quebec has provided a less favourable environment for immigrants than have most of the English speaking provinces. Accordingly, while a good many immigrants arrive with little knowledge of either of our official languages-
That is incorrect, but it is here in a so-called government white paper. There is only one official language in Canada.
-English is the language that is most often learned. This is an imbalance which the government-
He means ''cabinet".
-is anxious to correct by any practicable means.
In paragraph 40 the minister writes that immigration must be closely related to truly national objectives. Surely we are entitled to ask, is one of these national objectives going to be the forcing of immigrants into the area east of the Ottawa river in order that the cabinet may correct the imbalance between English speaking and French speaking people as outlined in paragraph 34?
In a ten-page memorandum outlining "A New Selection Policy for Immigration", dated April 10 and issued by the minister, it is stated:
Lastly, there is the question of where in the country the immigrant is going. If he is aiming at an area where employment prospects generally are strong, his chances of satisfactory settlement will be improved even if his qualifications are somewhat marginal.
On pages 3 and 4 of "Background Notes for White Paper on Immigration" the minister advised the House of Commons immigration committee:
In paragraph 34 it is stated that the government proposes to seek a solution to the imbalance existing at present in the integration of new arrivals into English and French speaking communities. One very important project which has recently been launched is an exhaustive study of the problems of adjustment facing new French speaking arrivals especially in French speaking communities with a view to attracting and holding more substantial numbers of French speaking immigrants. The first phase of this research program will involve interviewing in depth representative samples of French Canadians, fairly recently arrived French immigrants and lastly French speaking immigrants who for one reason or another have found it necessary to return to their native countries. This first phase will also involve an examination of the attitudes of French speaking populations toward emigration to Canada and to French Canada in particular. The second phase of the program is to consist of a larger study of French speaking immigrants designed to establish their geographic, occupational and job mobility patterns and to discover the underlying economic, social and psychological forces determining their attitudes.
Of possibly more immediate effect is a re-evaluation of our operations in France with a view to improving our capabilities there.

These statements clearly say that certain people seem determined to direct immigrants to that part of Canada east oi the Ottawa river, although members of parliament like the hon. member for Villeneuve keep rising in the House of Commons to ask why it is that unemployment statistics for the province of Quebec month after month and year after year are 35 per cent of the national unemployment total. These figures are borne out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics reports for December, 1966 and January, 1967. The four Atlantic provinces have an even greater proportion of unemployment than Quebec.
These two excerpts from the white paper on immigration clearly show a conflict in planning. In one sentence we are advised that if the immigrant is aiming at an area where employment prospects generally are strong his chances of satisfactory settlement will be good, while the second quotation intimates that the cabinet wants to increase the settlement of immigrants in provinces east of the Ottawa river where unemployment is high, in an effort to correct what is described as an imbalance between two tongues.
I have in my hand a statement showing the equalization payments made to the various provinces from 1959-60 to 1967-68. These so-called equalization payments run into millions of dollars, in the case of Quebec $260 million this year. These so-called equalization payments are based on provincial population. They are the payments that the Canadian government makes to the "have not" provinces, as they are described or as the Minister of Finance described them, as found in Hansard of March 9 of this year, the "less fortunate provinces." These equalization payments are made to the "have not" or the "less fortunate" provinces by the federal government by the simple expediency of withholding federal funds from what are known as the "have" provinces, namely, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
The table of figures which I received from the Department of Finance this very month shows clearly that every one of the five provinces east of the Ottawa river is a "have not" province or a "less fortunate province", in the words of the Minister of Finance. Yet according to the white paper on immigration we are to advance help and money to settle people in the "have not" provinces because they are east of the Ottawa river, rather than let them find their own way to the fortunate provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia which are described as "have" provinces for the basis of calculating equalization payments
May 25, 1967

Immigration Act
that are being made to some provinces which are not entitled to them at the present time and never have been entitled to them.
Now that the white paper on immigration has publicized the cabinet's evident desire to correct an imbalance in the populations speaking the two major languages in Canada,
I desire to know just how great this imbalance is supposed to be. Is it of such dimensions that it will take years of very heavy immigration to satisfy the desires of the cabinet, or is it of such minute proportions that the country might be expected to adjust the figures to the satisfaction of the administration in a short time? Are we going to refuse admission to Canada because of this so-called imbalance, of well educated and skilled persons who speak one language and give preference to people of another language even if their skills and education are not the equal of those would-be immigrants of another tongue? I am anxious to learn as soon as possible just how great an enterprise Canada is expected to take on in its efforts to correct this so-called imbalance.
For that reason I endeavoured this month to place a written question on the order paper of the House of Commons in an effort to ascertain just how serious a challenge has been made to Canada by the cabinet. Therefore I addressed this question to the Clerk of the House of Commons with the request that it be placed on the order paper: Question, May 8, 1967
In the white paper entitled "Canadian Immigration Policy. 1966" it is stated that "while a good many immigrants arrive with little knowledge . . . English is the language that is most often learned. This is an imbalance which the government is anxious to correct." What date in Canadian history was satisfactory to the present cabinet as the day on which the imbalance between French and English speaking peoples would have been satisfactory to the cabinet? Will this be the target of the cabinet's efforts as mentioned in paragraph 34 of the white paper?
You will be interested in the reply I received from the Clerk Assistant of the House of Commons:
When you ask what date in Canadian history was satisfactory to the present cabinet about a certain proposition it seems to me this is contrary to citation 171 (gg) which says that a question must not "seek information about matters which are in their nature secret, such as decisions or proceedings of cabinet, advice given to Crown by law officers, etc ..."
It seems to me also that the question is contrary to citation 171 (w) which says that a question must not "raise a matter of policy too large to be dealt with in the limits of an answer to a question."
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The white paper sets out policy, and although we know there is a white paper on immigration we never saw the policy which is set out in it before it was issued. The answer continues:
-your question is against Citation 171 (bb) which says that a question cannot be asked which "asks the government's opinion on matters of policy".
From this reply one realizes that Canada is expected to correct a situation mentioned by the cabinet of which we have not been given the dimensions. Is this a task which is going to occupy us during the remainder of our taxpaying years, or will our children and grandchildren have to slave to correct this imbalance which is as yet undefined?

Generally, French immigrants get more easily established in Quebec than in other provinces, but this does not mean that the majority choose to remain in Quebec. Rather, more of those French immigrants remain in Quebec, as compared to immigrants whose native tongue is not French.
The hon. member for Lapointe wanted to know why we are asking for that increase from $12 to $20 million. First of all, the house is aware that this fund is used for loans and not gifts, which means that the money loaned to immigrants is usually paid back within a period of 24 months.
But over the last few years immigration has increased tremendously, it has gone up from 75,000 people in 1962 to almost 200,000 this year and, according to available statistics, there will probably be an increase of 20 to 25 per cent this year, which means that nearly
250,000	immigrants will probably come here.
Therefore, because there are more immigrants, a greater number of them are using our loan program devised to assist the immigrant and his family with their transportation expenses. At the present time, over $10 million are tied up in loans which will, of course, be paid back to the government. But if we do not increase the amount in the fund from $12 to $20 million, within a few weeks, and possibly within a week, we will run short of money to make loans to immigrants who want to come to Canada under the accepted principles.
That is the only explanation, there is no other. It is not in view of a future policy, it is simply to continue the present program.
There is no doubt-and I think that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) understood it-that it is a very special amendment, that there is no question of reshaping government policy in the field of help to immigrants.
It is simply a question of enabling us now, before the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate makes its report, to continue our assistance to the immigrants coming to Canada under the program already adopted by the government and which has been operative for more than 15 years. I think it was implemented first in 1951 and has been amended a few times.
But he asked whether our intention was to implement the principles laid down in the white paper. I can assure the hon. member
Immigration Act
for Carleton that our intention is to extend this program to all countries of the world.
As he mentioned, these loans were extended only to immigrants from certain countries of Europe. Last year, it was extended to the people from the Caribbean and, as soon as we have the money, or the available funds and the facilities, we intend to extend it to all immigrants from any part of the world.
I make here a formal statement about it and I hope he will be satisfied; we are proceeding along that line, and I hope we will achieve our objective as early as possible.
From our estimates, if the amount is increased from $12 million to $20 million, we will have enough money to extend the program to any country, regardless of the immigrants' origin.
Obviously, one can say it is not a new policy; an opportunity to discuss it further will be provided when the joint committee report is submitted to the house. Then, we shall be in a position to discuss this angle and I shall be quite willing to do so. At present, however, if for one reason or another, the house refuses to increase this amount, it would not mean the end of Canada, of course, not even the end of our immigration policy, but it would mean that a certain number of immigrants would be denied the help offered to them.
Now, I do not want to take the house by surprise, but I intend to propose an amendment to the regulations about loans to immigrants.
This amendment deals with the interest rate. At present, these loans are granted to immigrants without interest. I do not think this is a good policy, and I want to explain why. At any rate, I do not believe that charging interest would reduce the number of immigrants to Canada. I do not believe the interest would be high enough for that. But, at the present time, we realize that more and more people take advantage of the plan, but there is nothing to show that they really need the money we lend them.
In other words, some immigrants with money, who could afEord to settle in Canada on their own, might take advantage of the plan, keep their own money and perhaps invest it at 6, 7 or 8 per cent interest, while obtaining from us interest-free loans.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that it is reasonable for us to charge interest-I intend to suggest a rate of 6 per cent-first of all, to encourage early repayment to the government and, in the second place, to limit the loans as

May 25, 1967
Immigration Act
much as possible to the immigrants who need them. I do not believe it would be fair to the Canadian taxpayers that an immigrant, having money, should come here with the help of an interest-free loan from us, which he could repay over a 24-month period. Therefore I think this is normal.
On the other hand, when we consider the federal aid-to-immigrants policy, Mr. Chairman, I would prefer a more generous set-up. That is if, at a given time, immigrants were needed and if some of them were really in financial straits it might be better then to give them money outright rather than to make loans to them.
At the outset, when the program was established some four per cent of the immigrants took advantage of our loan program. Today, that proportion has reached 25 per cent and when the scheme will become better known, every immigrant will probably try to obtain money from the government, which will add up to fabulous sums.
I therefore advise the house that I intend to ask the cabinet to allow a 6 per cent interest to be charged on those loans.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, some matters that are not at all relevant to the bill now before us have been brought up. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-106, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the grain growers of western Canada and their marketing agency, the Canadian Wheat Board, have made such a great contribution to the national economy and their methods of marketing are so highly and widely accepted in international grain trading circles as well as domestically that in this government's opinion the time has come to give more permanence to the legislation governing the operations of the wheat board. The board is now a permanent part of the
May 25, 1967

Canadian scene and the grain growers of the west wish it to be considered as such. I am therefore pleased to be able to bring to the attention of the house amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It is only a few months since the responsibility to parliament for the wheat board was assigned to me, but I am proud to be associated with this remarkable Canadian activity and would like to take this first opportunity to say a few words about it.
During the past few years the production and marketing of wheat have been at levels unprecedented in our history. During this period we have had the highest levels of production, exports, wheat prices and farm income ever recorded in the history of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The principal function of the Canadian Wheat Board is, of course, to sell the wheat, oats and barley delivered by western Canadian grain producers at the best possible prices. The Canadian Wheat Board has carried out its duties in a most efficient and successful manner. Equally, the government of the day has done everything in its power to assist the board in selling as large a volume of wheat as possible.
Let me review briefly the production and marketing performance of recent years. In the past four crop years wheat production has exceeded 2.8 billion bushels. This figure is 500 million bushels more than total wheat output in any other four-year period. Thus, we have had the equivalent of an extra crop to market in the past four years.
Demand in world markets has improved in recent years but, none the less, it has been a challenging task to market the tremendous quantities of wheat that were produced. I can remember vividly that when I was in the government prior to 1957, an export total in excess of 300 million bushels was considered a very good year indeed. In contrast, we have recently had two crop years with exports approaching 600 million bushels. The average for the past three years has been 525 million bushels compared with the average of 350 million bushels in the previous three years. In achieving these record wheat exports very heavy commitments were assumed but each challenge was met and Canada did not default on a single contract.
It should be emphasized that this large export movement was not at the expense of other grains. In 1965-66, overseas shipments of oats and barley were also higher than in 27053-37J

Canadian Wheat Board Act the previous year. In addition, the full requirement of our domestic market for feed grains was met.
On behalf of the government I should like to pay tribute to the grain producers, the Canadian Wheat Board, the Board of Grain Commissioners, the railways, the elevator companies, the brokers, the shippers and all the other organizations and individuals who did so much to make this achievement possible.
In reviewing the recent record of wheat marketing, it is of value to examine the various components which contribute to the very impressive total.
Nearly half of Canada's wheat and flour exports are now shipped to Sino-Soviet countries, to most of whom it is necessary to extend credit in order to do business. The policy of selling wheat on government assisted credit terms was implemented 15 years ago when 5.5 million bushels of wheat were sold to Yugoslavia under section 21 of the Export Credits Insurance Act. Since that time Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Hungary, Mainland China and East Germany have purchased large quantities of Canadian wheat on credit terms. Taken together, these countries represent a market for over 20 per cent of our total exports. In recent years, credit sales have been confined to countries prepared to enter into long-term purchase and supply agreements and, with the exception of the U.S.S.R., all countries entering into such agreements have availed themselves of Canadian government credit facilities under either the Export Credits Insurance Act or the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The government has made these exports possible by assuming credit risks which today amount to more than $500 million compared with $200 million in 1962.
The Canada-U.S.S.R. trade agreement, which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) negotiated 11 years ago, was the first long-term agreement with a Sino-Soviet country involving the purchase and supply of Canadian wheat. The U.S.S.R. has been by far the largest purchaser of Canadian wheat under long-term arrangements. Mainland China is the second largest purchaser of Canadian wheat under long-term arrangements. Many of the long-term wheat agreement negotiators have been conducted concurrently with or as part of trade agreement negotiations. Wheat has, therefore, made its contribution to the broadening of trade in other commodities.
57G
May 25. 1967

Canadian Wheat Board Act
In 1966 I visited the U.S.S.R. and a number of eastern European countries-Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslovia, Bulgaria, Hungary- and returned encouraged by prospects for continuation of substantial sales to this area for many years to come.
In recent years the publicity attracted by the large quantities of grain we have sold to Sino-Soviet block countries has tended to overshadow the importance we attach to purchases made by our traditional markets such as Britain, Japan, West Germany, Italy, Belgium and Venezuela. Canada sells wheat and flour to almost 100 countries, and I can assure the house that during the recent period of strong demand the needs of our traditional customers, both large and small, were taken into account before other commitments were undertaken.
There is one development in wheat marketing in Canada, which has certainly not received the attention I think it merits. I refer to our food aid program. The allocation of funds for food aid in the form of wheat and flour has increased substantially in the last few years, rising from about $4.5 million in the 1962-63 fiscal year to an exceptional level of about $100 million in the last fiscal year, reflecting Canada's contribution to meeting emergency needs in India. In the years ahead Canada will continue to be a major supplier of food aid. Canadians can take great pride in the fact that, on a per capita basis, we are now as large a contributor of wheat and flour aid as any country in the world.
Hon. members are aware that western grain producers attach the greatest importance to international co-operation in grain marketing. The Canadian government supported by representatives of western farm organizations has taken the lead in seeking acceptable international agreements for wheat embodied in the successive international wheat agreements. We have again played a central role in the successful negotiations of the key elements of a new three year agreement providing a significantly higher price range for wheat, of which I was pleased to inform the house on May 15. This news was significant not only to those directly involved in the production of wheat but to all Canadians because of the importance of wheat exports to our whole economy.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
As I stated previously, the newly agreed price range involves a 21-cent increase in both the minimum and the maximum price for No. 1 Northern over the current I.W.A.

price range which expires on July 31. The new minimum for No. 1 Northern is $1.95J in store the Lakehead and $2.03J f.o.b. Vancouver. The price range is 40 cents U.S. or approximately 43 cents Canadian, making the new maximums $2,384 in store the Lakehead and $2.46J f.o.b. Vancouver. In addition to increased minimum and maximum prices the new agreement provides for a considerable strengthening of the minimum price systems, representing a significant improvement over the international wheat agreement.
In contrast to the I.W.A. which specified a minimum and a maximum price for only No. 1 Northern, the new price schedule identifies ten major grades of wheat with agreed minimum and maximum prices. These wheats include No. 1 and No. 3 Northern from Canada, four U.S. grades of wheat and one each from Australia, Argentina, the E.E.C. and Sweden. This new schedule provides greater assurance of equivalent obligations by all exporting countries in complying with the objective of price stability and the observance of minimum prices.
The difficulties involved in reaching agreement on the price relationships between these grades proved insoluble throughout the history of the international wheat agreements. They have been overcome, however, in this agreement by establishing substantially strengthened price consultative procedures. I should emphasize that each grade of wheat may compete freely within the price range. The scheduled minimum prices for the various types of wheat can only be modified by agreement.
In addition to the improved price schedules, the establishment of a multilateral food aid program represents an unprecedented advance in assuring continuing supplies of wheat, flour and other grains for needy countries and providing at the same time a more equitable sharing of this cost among developed countries, both those exporting and importing grains. The total annual program agreed to by the 17 countries involved in this stage of the negotiation was 4.5 million metric tons of wheat and/or coarse grains suitable for human consumption. Canada's contribution of one-half million tons represents 11 per cent of the total and is second only to the United States which is providing 42 per cent of the program.
The agreement reached in Geneva was negotiated by the major grain trading countries participating in the Kennedy round, this
May 25, 1967

Canadian Wheat Board Act
is, 11 countries plus the E.E.C. The 11 countries are Switzerland, Denmark, Norway, Japan, Australia, Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Argentina, Sweden and Finland. Negotiations are now being directed toward bringing other countries interested in trade in wheat, both GATT and non-GATT members, into this agreement and to set up the machinery to bring the agreement into effect as soon as possible.
The major exporters and importers agreed in Geneva to work diligently for the early completion of negotiations which will broaden the agreement reached there to include all countries interested in trade in wheat. It is anticipated, of course, that it will take a little time to tie up all the ends of this agreement and it may not become operative until early next year. Hon. members will recall that the price provisions of the present international wheat agreement expire July 31. On the matter of price, it is understood in trade terms that this means the new price range which I have reported to the house will be observed in the months ahead until the new agreement becomes fully effective. Canadian selling prices are currently about 17 cents above the new agreed minimum prices. It has been agreed by Kennedy round signatories that nothing in the subsequent negotiations shall prejudice the price and food aid commitments entered into by them.
The successful outcome of these negotiations within the Kennedy round was due in no small measure to the continuing presence and advice of the advisory committee to the wheat board and the participation of Canadian Wheat Board officials as part of the Canadian delegation in Geneva.
Following the harvest of the largest wheat crop in Canadian history in 1966 wheat supplies in Canada totalled almost 1.3 billion bushels, a new record. It is obvious that we must continue to strive for the largest possible volume of exports. It seems clear that in the years ahead there will be an increasing demand for Canadian wheat. This is not to say that there will not be some years when a reduction in demand could create marketing problems. Wheat selling is a highly competitive business and I would not want to create the impression that there will be no problems in marketing Canadian wheat. Each year presents a different marketing situation. The Canadian Wheat Board has served the western producer well in the past and I know hon. members will share my view that the board will be equal to challenges as they develop in the coming years.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to return to the main purpose for seeking amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. As the act now stands its administrative powers as set forth in sections 23, 24 and 34 will expire August 1, 1967. It has been customary to renew them for periods of five years. It is now decided to ask parliament to make the board's powers permanent. It has become the practice of the board to enter into agreements for the supply of grain over extended periods of time and, as I have already mentioned, nearly one-half of our exports of wheat and flour are now marketed under long-term arrangements of this type. These buyers naturally expect the wheat board's powers to cover the full period of these longterm agreements, and making them permanent meets this point as well as recognizing the de facto situation of the industry and its selling agency. This proposed amendment will, therefore, formally recognize what has been apparent to producers and buyers alike for many years and will, I believe, give effect to their wishes which in many instances have been expressed.
Accordingly I recommend the adoption of these simple amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the principal one being to extend the powers of the board, which would otherwise expire. The first amendment specifies that the governor in council shall designate the minister responsible to parliament for the operations of the board. In the present act the minister is specifically designated as the Minister of Agriculture. This amendment will provide more flexibility in that respect. Section 23 of the present Canadian Wheat Board Act provides that the provisions of part II of the act will be repealed on and after the 1st day of August, 1967. Section 34 of the act provides that the provisions of part IV will also be repealed on and after the 1st day of August, 1967. The repeal of these sections places the powers of the board on a permanent basis. There is also an amendment to section 24 as a consequence of the repealing of sections 23 and 34. The schedule of mills and feed warehouses mentioned in section 45 is also being revised to bring it up to date.

He then goes on to suggest that Canada is going to have some difficulty in meeting her share of world wheat requirements.
During the past few months speeches have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) suggesting that before long all of the food requirements of this country will be produced by a decreasing percentage of the Canadian population. I think the figure both ministers quoted was 5 per cent. I am not prepared to quarrel with that figure; it may well be correct, depending on the population of the country. But I do want to emphasize that this does not necessarily mean that we are going to have fewer farmers. Indeed, as I said earlier, I think that if we are to take full advantage of our production potential we must get away from the idea that the way to increase productivity is through the use of absentee or corporate farmers. This type of farmer, though he may be able to show the best return on his investment, is not the type of farmer who is going to produce the most food for the world. Attention must be paid to the farmer who knows the land best and who can best increase the productivity of a given area.
This concept involves many things. First of all, there is need for legislation to ensure that young people are given a start in farming, and at the present time there is not even a remote possibility of this. What happens is that when an older farmer retires the land is almost invariably bought by someone else who already has a large establishment in operation. Some attention must be given to the need to ensure that the moderate-size farm, the sort of family farm that the farm organizations have been talking about for the last number of years, is given some chance of survival.
Some changes in the quota system will also be required. The type of quota system now existing is of some advantage to larger farms but does not give small farms of 400 to 600 acres the advantage they should have. I would not recommend the use of the type of quota system which was adopted yesterday in admitting people to the House of Commons. What is required is a type of system which will slightly improve the opportunities of the small farmer. I am convinced that it is only the person who works very closely with the soil, who understands its capabilities and maximizes his opportunities for production, who can assist this country and the world in 
meeting the needs with which we will be faced in the next 20 years.
I should like to make one suggestion to the minister which is based on experience in the United States. When that country's administration attempted to limit production it found out that the United States farmer was ingenious enough to be able to overcome all the restrictions imposed upon him and increase his production. Perhaps this is one way to get maximum production, Mr. Speaker-by imposing limitations. I think this gives an indication of the ability of the farmer to increase his production despite limitations which are imposed upon him.
There must also be better utilization of land resources as well as of human and financial resources. I think of research into new varieties of coarse grains, for example. It seems to me there should be a shifting of the available acreage from the growing of coarse grains to wheat production, as well as an improvement in the variety of coarse grains. I understand that at the present time some of the research stations are developing a feed grain that can produce up to 200 bushels an acre. This sort of procedure will enable us to remove many acres which are suited to wheat growing from the production of coarse grain. We shall be able to produce many bushels of feed grain to meet the increasing future demand in this country for feed grains.

We must have improvements in transportation and harbour facilities and we must improve the methods of getting grain from the farm on to the ships. The committee on agriculture studied this question intensively this past spring and recommended improvements. I hope the government will pay attention to those recommendations which may improve some of the problems plaguing transportation.
If proper steps are taken to meet the anticipated wheat demand in the years to come the government will be rewarded by the farmers who play an important part in the economy of our country. More than once in the last few years the prairie farmers have saved the government from difficult balance of payments situations. That should be remembered. The increased grain marketing have had a beneficial result in eastern Canada, because as a result of increased marketings and improved prices the farmers were able to improve production methods and to buy fertilizers and machines for their operations. Canada has benefited greatly by the increased wheat
May 25, 1967

sales of the last few years. The minister mentioned the figures, and we can all be proud of what the western farmers have done for the country.
We should not adopt the position taken by the Globe and Mail that the best way to reduce surpluses is to lower prices. That is what the Globe and Mail recommends that the dairy farmers should do, and it is so much outdated nonsense. Wheat surpluses did not disappear with lower prices. Nobody benefits from lower prices, and we must make sure that the people of this country realize that surpluses of wheat are not a burden but a blessing. The cost of storing surplus wheat is only a fraction of the cost which the housewife would have to meet if there was a shortage in this country. It should be remembered that the money spent to assist in the marketing of wheat benefits not so much the producer as the consumer of this country, and the consumer ought to be aware of that. Money spent in ensuring a stable supply of food is actually money saved.
In conclusion, I hope that by making this legislation permanent the government will not be precluded from examining it periodically. I looked at the schedule and saw that it listed out of date facts. Canadian Wheat Board Act are of the opinion that the world wheat requirements will reach four billion bushels by 1980 and this will require quite a large increase in production. However, delivery of the grain would have to be undertaken in a very short time. I do not think this is a very practical suggestion. They had been promised something in the nature of a two-price system, but hoped that increased sales of wheat on the international market would make this unnecessary. However, with a 21-cent increase in the price of wheat I am sure they are looking for some action in this regard.
In recent years there has been argument about whether the wheat board has been fully responsible for Canada's increased sales of wheat. I take some exception to the suggestion that they have. I give credit to the board for what they have done so far, but I do not think the sale of wheat abroad has reached the level which we might expect. In this regard it might be helpful if our export credit program was very much increased in respect of the underdeveloped countries. I understand this principle was instrumental in bringing about the first and very large sale to Red China. If the wheat board received full cooperation from the Minister of Finance on this matter, I am sure that the sale of wheat on the international market could be greatly expanded. Canada is very fortunate because I suppose we are still the largest owner of undeveloped land. We have on the farm, certainly on farms of western Canada, the potential for greatly increased production.
May 25, 1967

I think the government could provide financial assistance to the farmers in another way. For instance, it might be better, in respect of the potash which we are exporting, if preferred loans were made in order that the potash might be used on our own bleached-out soil. This type of financial assistance to the farmers would pay off in our national economy.
I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) make another plea for the family farm. Unless I am mistaken, it is the policy of this government that the family farm must go and that nothing but the large corporation outfits will operate in future. Nothing could be further from the truth. I think Canada will always need a large population based on the farm. The only way we can keep the family farm going, in view of the fact that there is a movement away from agriculture today, is by doing everything possible to encourage the small farmer to stay on the farm. I would go even further than that and say we should have many more small farms in this country.
I do not think financing is the bottle-neck. I think the price the farmer gets for his grain is one aspect of the problem. The expanded markets of the world are there if we go after them, and if we increased our sales in these markets it would solve much of the problem. I have every confidence that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) will pursue this matter. I do not want him to be shy in this regard. He is apparently doing a good job in his department. We would like to see cabinet solidarity at least in this field. If the minister can get together with the Minister of Finance and any other minister who can help expand Canada's markets and exports generally, we will be the first to congratulate him. As you can see tonight, Mr. Speaker, there is unanimity in this party. We are encouraging the forward-looking type of approach which we are apparently getting from this department. That is why I am perhaps stretching the patience of the Chair a little in suggesting that, surrounding the policy in respect of the wheat board, there are these other facets of marketing and price control which will assist the small farmer to stay on the farm. In this way we will be able to provide a shot in the arm for the whole Canadian economy.
