I would be glad to do that, Mr. Chairman. At the outset I wish to thank all hon. members for their participation in this debate and the very complimentary remarks that I take to be directed to the wheat board. I will see that they are passed on to the proper source. I share this high regard for the wheat board, and in the short time in which I have been associated with them that high regard has been enhanced. They have done a marvellous job of marketing and selling wheat in over 100 countries in the world and have left no stone unturned in seeking out opportunities to sell more wheat. Where the matter of credit is involved, as my hon. friend from Athabasca said, they are not at all shy in asking the government to extend the amount required.
I cannot think of a single instance where we have lost a sale because of lack of credit facilities. The first large sale to China was, as was quite properly said, negotiated by the wheat board under the previous government on the basis of large credit facilities made available under the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
That pattern has been followed by a subsequent sale to China. In the other socialist countries in Europe the facilities for credit are being used, except in the case of Russia which continues to pay cash. Of course, we are very pleased about it.
The other important question has to do with the recommendation of the committee on agriculture relating to whether or not the important commodities of rye, flax and rape seed should be included under the provisions of this statute. This is a matter to which I have given considerable attention in the short time that I have been responsible for the wheat board. I have not concluded my consideration. The wheat board would find it quite a different sort of operation from the selling of wheat, oats and barley with respect to which Canada's position in the markets of the world is quite dominant, important, and over
May 25, 1967

Canadian Wheat Board Act the price structure of which we can exercise an influence and have some control. Rye, rape seed and flax are quite different. The role that Canada could play in these commodities is relatively insignificant in the markets of the world. We would not have the same opportunities to influence price or to help bring about orderly marketing. We would be more apt to be carried along by the price structure in the world rather than have the opportunity of playing a role in establishing it, which is a function that the wheat board now discharges very well. I have had a great many representations on both sides of this question by people who feel that here is one area in which they could use their own private initiative to good advantage, and many have done so, as hon. members of this house know so well.
I am naturally impressed by the recommendations of the committee on agriculture and I would like to give them full consideration. I think an important fact is that all of us have been deeply involved recently in the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations. The commissioners of the wheat board have attended regularly at Geneva and devoted all their energies and time to the sale and agreements for the future sale of wheat and, in a different area, to the sale of oats and barley. Moreover, the concentration has been and will be on wheat for some time to come until all the details of the current agreement are worked out and it becomes operative. So, it will be some time before I and those who are responsible for advising me can come to a definitive conclusion on this important matter. But I can tell all hon. members that this is very much on our minds and we will not lose sight of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was quite pleased to hear at least one remark made by the minister, although I do not disagree with the other ones. I was pleased to hear that he has been reading the report of the committee on agriculture, and therefore I might conclude that it has raised in his mind the same problem that arises in mine, namely that the amendment which is before us in two parts is a very small, insignificant and uncontentious one. However, there were a number of things which the committee was able to learn about the operations of the wheat board and which were unknown to most of the members of the committee. I believe that if we are only going to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act once a year, some of the amendments to the act which have been recommended by the committee members should be included. The explanation of the first clause concerning the 
designation of a minister by the governor in council was made the subject of some recommendations in the committee. While I am sure there is a great deal of merit in making the person responsible for the wheat board the one who has the best knowledge of the wheat board, this appointment is subject to change, and rather unusual arrangements have had to be made at times in designating the minister responsible for the wheat board.
The minister made what appeared to me, and I think to the committee, a rather controversial point regarding what the Canadian Wheat Board can do about the problems of sale expansion and the obvious intention of the farmers to go into the production of oil seed crops as well. The fact is that we are annually doubling the previous year's production with no end in sight. However, the difficulty arises with the sales. As regards rape-seed, reports in the newspapers last year caused considerable consternation among the farmers. They indicated that the sale price of one particular shipment had gone up very rapidly and yet the same increase was not reflected in any other sales. When the committee investigated the matter, they found that this very large increase in the sale price of that particular shipment was an unusual circumstance which was not likely to be repeated. My assessment of the briefs that were presented with regard to this matter led me to believe that most of the farmers were of the opinion that the wheat board, in the marketing of grain in general not only of wheat, has some say in the selling price of that commodity because it has such a large amount for export purposes. The minister is perfectly right when he says that Canada is the leader in wheat sales in the world's markets.
An amendment made to the Canadian Wheat Board Act a few years ago placed oats and barley under the wheat board, although in a different category than wheat. It seems to me that this operation is rather confused when one realizes that the grain exchange does deal in futures for oats and barley which are not handled in exactly the same way as wheat. I think most of the farmers in western Canada agree that the operations of the wheat board with regard to the sale of oats and barley have been advantageous to the farmers and have placed Canada in a position in the world markets where we were able to provide facilities which have brought a certain amount of stability to the coarse grain field. I am sure most of the farmers agree
May 25, 1967	COMMONS
that probably the operation that will be undertaken by the wheat board with regard to rapeseed and other oil seeds will not be the same as that undertaken with regard to coarse grains or wheat but that the national marketing agency with its connections all across the world will be in a much better position to sell advantageously, as far as the farmer is concerned, the oil seed crops which have been produced in increasing amounts by the farmers in western Canada.
If the minister is of the opinion that the recommendations against bringing rapeseed under the act outweighed those in favour of it, I would say that I think these representations were mostly made by Mr. McNamara. He is very much opposed to bringing rapeseed under the board for the simple reason that this would involve a change in the policy of the board and of the sales agents across the world. There is no question that they would have to operate in a totally different manner since that commodity would only be a small part of the total sales. It is also true, as the minister said, that decisions of the wheat board may be subjected to undue influence by the major producers in the oil seed field.
I think it is fair to say that most of the members of the committee were not opposed to the operation which is now being undertaken by the grain exchange in the futures of oil seed. I noticed that in the last few days the price of silver on the stock market in Canada and the U.S. was only allowed to go up five cents a day. In London, on the other hand, the price of silver jumped up 14 or 15 cents in one day. I understand that there is a daily limit to any price increase of rapeseed which is part of our grain exchange strucutre. Therefore, I think the problem we used to face in the trading of futures on exchanges to some extent has been curtailed. If we are able to operate satisfactorily in terms of wheat, barley and oats, then I think we should be able to do the same with other seed products.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Stability in rapeseed production is very necessary to agriculture, and it will have a great effect in a number of ways. It used to be argued by those who represent, for instance, soybean interests and other oil seed producers in eastern Canada, that the government should not permit rapid expansion of the oil seed industry in the west. I think obviously because they would be affected by it. However, it is true that as the oil seed industry expands we will be in a much better position nationally to provide the oils that are
DEBATES	589
Canadian Wheat Board Act required to produce soap, margarine-particularly margarine-and other commodities.
It appears, Mr. Chairman, that if we are to protect both of these industries, then it would be of advantage if the national marketing agency in western Canada also had some control over the sale of the end products, as well as the preparation of sales estimates in the markets of the world to which the representatives of the wheat board pay close attention. It would then be possible to advise the farmers, as is the case with other commodities, how much they may expect to receive when they harvest their crop.
For this reason I think that, in bringing forward this bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the minister would be remiss if he did not refer it to the committee in order to consider the advisability of including these commodities. 1 do not think it is sufficient merely to listen to representations. The arguments used by the wheat board in this regard were, I think, very weak. I think the arguments put forward by the grain exchange and the grain trade, which were not unlike the arguments advanced by the wheat board, carried much more weight, because although they admitted it might be possible to include these other oil seed products, they pointed out that certain problems would result. They recognized that other conditions would have to be met and other concessions would have to be made.
I think this states the position much more realistically. Things have now got to the stage in western Canada where the production of oil seed per acre is so much more profitable than the production of wheat that oil seed products are steadily and rapidly increasing in volume. For that reason, before we reach the stage of saturation, I think we should develop the controls that are necessary.
I realize that this bill was introduced for the specific purpose of beating the deadline and establishing the wheat board as a permanent body, a step with which I think everyone is in agreement. We are all concerned as to whether we should review the act every five years. Since I have been here, the activities of the wheat board have been reviewed many times and under different circumstances; its operations have been reviewed annually in the committee as well as in other forums. But the question always arises whether the activities of the wheat board should be annually reviewed in the committee, or should be reviewed every five years under some form of major overhaul when the
May 25, 1967

Canadian Wheat Board Act deadline arrives. I think it is necessary to decide whether or not we want to dispense with this terminal date and make the board a permanent body. I do not think there is any argument about that.
The one point I should like to make in this regard is that this is marketing type of legislation which is subject to fluctuation in production and ability to sell agricultural products. Therefore, I think there should be some sort of major overhaul and review of this act along the lines of the decennial revision of the Bank Act. Nevertheless, I think all hon. members will support the principle of making the wheat board a permanent body, rather than having to meet this deadline every five years as is the case at present.
I have glanced at the bill but I did not notice a date proposed therein. Therefore, I presume that the board is being made permanent without our making the review that I think is necessary. The minister may be quite right in contending that the annual review made by the committee under its statutory referral is sufficient, but nevertheless I think the minister should give serious consideration to some of the problems which have arisen in relation to the wheat board.
In this regard, I think the members of the committee are to be highly commended for the work they did. I have been a member of the agricultural committee for eight or nine years, and I do not think it is unfair to say that each time the committee has reviewed the report of the wheat board most members had not the faintest notion what it was all about.
For example, Mr. Chairman, there always seemed to be a political difference of opinion over who in fact sold our wheat, whether the credit should go to the government or to the wheat board. I was very surprised to find that technically neither the government nor the wheat board should be given the credit. Our agents really make sales of wheat on behalf of Canada, and this was fairly evident in the last sale that we made to Russia.
A number of matters were highlighted during our discussions to which I think the minister will have to pay some attention because the problems are immediate. We are now greatly increasing wheat production in western Canada. It is possible that western Canada may produce a billion bushels a year, and if this is the case obviously we would be unable to handle it. Hon. members will recall being asked to take drastic legislative action 
to deal with a short-lived strike in two segments of the industry because the industry was operating at top capacity. If the volume is increasing yearly by another 400 million bushels, then we simply would not have the facilities to handle it.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the recommendations made particularly by the grain commissioners warrant consideration by the minister. I believe that the decision as to who should take the extra responsibility which is envisaged is a political one. The minister may decide that the wheat board can expand its activities into another field and empower the wheat board to make recommendations. It may be that the grain commissioners will be given a broader and more important role to play in projecting production and surveying the need for facilities to cope with increasing production. Or again, the minister may decide that another agency entirely should be established. On an occasion such as this, when the Wheat Board Act comes up for discussion I think the minister should assure the country that he will give consideration to these other questions, because they certainly affect the industry and have caused a great deal of concern in western Canada. It was not right for us to work so close to capacity that hysteria would break out as soon as anything untoward developed. We ought to be able to ship our wheat via our railways to the harbours, and enable every farmer to sell his crop. That, of course, has happened. I have in mind all the grain that we shipped in the last season, and I ask the government to pay attention to the committee's recommendations. We worked close to capacity, and the committee made some sensible suggestions. I think the minister would be well advised to refer this matter to the committee for further study. Should any legislation evolve from the committee's study, it would meet with the approval of the government and the country.

the second reading of Bill No. S-6, to revise and consolidate the Interpretation Act and amendments thereto, and to effect certain consequential amendments to the Canada Evidence Act and the Bills of Exchange Act.
He said:

Mr. Speaker, as an introduction to the debate on second reading of Bill No. S-6 to revise and consolidate the Interpretation Act, I think it will be enough for me to make a few very brief remarks.
Everyone knows, and the members of this house know it to a high degree, the role played by an Interpretation Act in a system of statutory rights. An interpretation act is, so to speak, a basic tool, the cornerstone of a system of statutory rights which facilitates not only the understanding thereof but its drafting. In a society like ours, Mr. Speaker, where we are more and more enclosed in a framework of laws and regulations, where we live in a very complex world regulated by a network of laws also complex, the legislator must strive to simplify as much as possible the system of laws and make their interpretation easier.
That is why an Interpretation Act was enacted as the first chapter of the statutes of the first Canadian parliament, a century ago, as a sort of preamble to all subsequent legislation and statutes to be passed in the future. Of course, Mr. Speaker, in the past century, a great number of amendments have been made to the Interpretation Act and now and then, those amendments have been incorporated in

May 25, 1967
Interpretation Act
consolidations of revised statutes which have been published, but this is the first time in a hundred years that legislator has fully reviewed that Interpretation Act and introduced a number of new definitions. He has also added to that act modern rules not only with regard to drafting but also to analysis and understanding which had been accepted by our parliaments and our courts at various periods.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Therefore, I wish to point out that this Interpretation Act somewhat recasts the form and subject matter of the former Interpretation Act. This bill has now been under study for around ten years by the officials of the Department of Justice. It was introduced to parliament in 1962 and reintroduced on several occasions during various sessions of various parliaments but, every single time, as a result of an adjournment or prorogation of the houses, it came to naught.
Mr. Speaker, the house is familiar with the bill under study, since it is very much the same as was approved last March by the permanent committee on justice and legal affairs. It differs very little from that bill. In a while, I shall indicate what changes were made. The bill now before the house was passed by the Senate, after going through the three stages, and we have now reached the motion for second reading in the House of Commons.

This bill having been through all three stages in the Senate, I hope we shall be able to deal with it fairly quickly. It is the same bill as was referred back by the standing committee on justice and legal affairs last March; it is the same bill, with four or five slight modifications. Perhaps I shall have a chance to deal with these differences later when we examine the matter clause by clause.
I can only plead with the house to consider this as a matter of some urgency. The commission which parliament set up two years ago to revise the statutes cannot bring its work to fruition until parliament has adopted this Interpretation Act, since the act does contain definitions and interpretations which are essential to the interpretation of statute law.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I commend the minister on the introduction tonight of his first piece of major legislation. After 
all, the Interpretation Act is, as he has indicated, the foundation upon which rest many of the other bills with which parliament has to deal. The hon. gentleman comes to the house with a reputation as being a small "1" liberal. I believe he will have many opportunities to deal along those lines with other legislation introduced by the government from time to time. We need this kind of approach, within reason.
I gather there have been some inconsequential changes, as a result of which the bill before us differs in some respects from the bill which was considered by the Senate and by the standing committee. I was not a member of the standing committee but I have had an opportunity to look up the record and read some of the observations made during the debates in the other place and before the standing committee. Basically, this is a matter of housekeeping, of tidying up, of making certain changes in the right context.
In addition, the bill probably takes note of certain decisions of the courts in connection with interpretation which the government and its advisers have felt should be reflected in its provisions for the sake of greater clarity; where there is one road which might be taken, the government wishes a particular road to be pointed out.
There is one clause in this bill, however, to which I must object. I will deal with it now, and invite the minister to indicate his view when he closes the debate. I know that my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), who was a member of the committee, feels as I do about this particular clause. He had hoped to be here this evening; indeed, he was here until the supper recess. I shall not go into details now; there will be an opportunity to do that when we get into committee. But I must refer to clause 2, the clause which purports to define regulations and enactments, in order to make my point plain. It would probably be best to read what is set out under 2(c) and 2(e).
(c) "enactment" means an Act or a regulation or any portion of an Act or regulation ...
(e) "regulation" includes an order, regulation, order in council, order prescribing regulations, rule, rule of court, form, tariff of costs or fees, letters patent, commission, warrant, proclamation, by-law, resolution or other instrument issued, made or established
(i)	in the execution of a power conferred by or under the authority of an Act, or
(ii)	by or under the authority of the Governor in Council.
During the discussion in the committee my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka
May 25, 1967

raised this point and one of the learned counsel from the department-I think it was the associate deputy minister-gave an explanation and an assurance to the committee, a( 9:20 p.m.)
The subject of the objection and of the doubt raised in the committee was the effect of this amendment (e) (ii) to give the authority to the Governor in Council to enact regulations without the authority of statute. This is the point that concerns a great many members of the House because we have seen a great many illustrations of it in the last year or so. The associate deputy minister replied that in his view, and he gave an assurance to that effect, this did not have the result of enacting substantive law and of giving to the government rights which it did not possess previously. This is the way I read the exchanges which took place between the witness and hon. members.
But, Mr. Speaker, that might be good enough for the committee. They did not pursue it to any great extent. However, quite honestly it is not good enough for me. I want to know what rights does the government now contend exist in the Governor in Council to enact regulations and orders in council not under the authority of statutes. It may well be that there have been cases where the extent to which the Governor in Council could exercise the opportunity to enact regulations, without this right being founded on a statute, has been in doubt. The effect of this amendment might well be to settle such doubt, to settle at least any anxieties which the government may have with regard to this right, a right to which I take the strongest possible exception unless it comes under the age old prerogative and of section 12 of the B.N.A. Act to which I will refer later. If it is the case that through this amendment the government is not seeking to secure the right to enact regulations and orders in council without doing so under the authority of a statute, then why was it necessary to include this amendment (e) (ii)? This is the point that puzzles me. It is my view, and I think the view of a lot of other members and of a lot of people in this country, that governments are powerful enough in this day and age without the authority to encroach on the rights of individuals without parliament having given .governments the right to do so by specific terms, by definite intent, and by definite words in a statute. I cannot conceive of any other circumstances under which the Governor in Council is so entitled to enact regulations and orders in council, and if that be the
Interpretation Act
case then the question the minister must answer is why was it necessary to add this particular amendment.
I recognize that there are a number of cases where parliament gives to the Governor in Council, to other boards, or to a minister, the right to issue regulations or to enact orders in council. In such cases the Governor in Council, tribunal or minister has the right to do so, and may directly enact regulations and orders in council which come within the Interpretation Act, it being a statute.
But that cannot be done unless there is a statute authorizing it, and if this is the case then I have to repeat myself: why was this amendment included?
Section 12 of the British North America Act is a very interesting section. I shall not read it in full because the minister is probably well aware of it. It states that all powers, authorities and functions which under any act of the parliament of Great Britain or of the parliament of the United Kingdom were vested in or exercisable by the governors or lieutenant governors of the provinces at the time of confederation, or which were capable of being exercised in a similar way by the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, would be continued in being and could be exercised by the Governor in Council of the newly formed country. But these were still rights which were exercised under a statute. The British North America Act is a statute, and my argument is that if the Governor in Council purports to act in any way not under the authority of a statute which this parliament has passed since confederation, then he can only do so under the authority of section 12 of the B.N.A. Act.
Quite simply my argument is that there is no justification or explanation for the addition of this particular amendment. We had an example of this matter not so long ago. A colleague of the minister, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), came before us at the tag end of last session, and for reasons which I do not attribute as being his fault, asked us in effect to approve in a retroactive way payments of money which the minister and the government had made under an order in council not pursuant to statute. This was with respect to the adult occupational training act. I am not sure that is its exact title, but hon. members will recall it.
On April 1, under an arrangement which had been made, the minister set machinery in motion by which he started paying out

May 25. 1967
Interpretation Act
certain moneys of the taxpayers of this country to people and to provinces. He did so, purporting to act under the authoritiy of an order in council passed pursuant to an appropriation bill or pursuant to supplementary estimates-I am not sure which. But, Mr. Speaker, the order in council which was passed was not passed pursuant to a specific statute of this parliament.
Despite that fact, it was not until May 8, when this house met to complete the final measures required for prorogation, that royal assent was given to the bill, thus for the first time giving authority to the minister and to the government to pay out these moneys. That was a flagrant illustration of the government passing an order in council without authority to do so, save by the very tenuous right of being enacted under an appropriations bill, with the result that the government had to come back to parliament five or six weeks later and ask for approval of the legislation.
This is the kind of thing which we have to worry about and be concerned about. It is for this reason I raise this matter and ask the minister to deal with it before we complete our consideration of this bill.
If the minister advises me that it is not the government's intention by this amendment to carve out for itself, or for any succeeding governments, the right to enact regulations and orders in council unless with the authority of a statute, then I would ask him to make that plain by an appropriate amendment. If, in fact, what the associate deputy minister said is the intention of the government, then I would suggest a simple amendment which the minister could consider between now and the time when we get into committee.
I would suggest he consider adding the following words after (e)(ii): "provided that this bill does not purport to convey or to grant to the Governor in Council the right to enact regulations save when authorized by statute." At this stage I am not trying to indicate the form of any amendment which might be moved, but if the government's view corresponds with what I think the law should be, and with what I think the associate deputy minister attempted to convey to the committee, the minister could make this quite plain by an amendment of this kind which would set at rest the doubts and anxieties which hon. members have with regard to the provision in (e)(ii).
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, this may seem to be highly technical and tenuous, but believe me it is not. All over the world we see examples where the lights of freedom are flickering out and where constitutional governments are being replaced by military or other forms of dictatorship. We think, because we have the right of freedom to assemble here as representatives of the people, that this type of thing cannot happen. It seems to me that all too often we tend to turn our parliament into a stage across which people posture and strut dealing with what might be entertainment issues without getting down to the nuts and bolts-the real issues-of democracy. All too often we let these things pass without prying into them. Then, at a later date, we wake up to find that the rights of the individual citizen have been filched away. Before this bill passes I think the government should provide an answer to this particular aspect of it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the second time today my remarks will be brief. First I should like to indicate my support of the plea made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) that we be given a clear understanding concerning what the government has in mind and what can be read into the new definition of a regulation to which reference has been made. I realize that the explanatory notes which tell us what this clause 2 is all about are very disarming. There is a two sentence paragraph which I should like to read. It appears opposite clause 2 of the bill:
The definitions of "Act", "enactment" and "regulation" are new.
Well, we know that.
Their purpose is to apply the whole of the Act to all orders in council and to the various instruments made under the authority of statutes.
That is vague, but it is disarming to suggest that the purpose here is simply to make sure that anything that is done by way of regulation must conform to the principles and rules laid down in the new Interpretation Act. In the process of doing this we are being asked to give, as the hon. member for Peace River has pointed out, what seems to be an extension of the power to doing things by order in council. Perhaps there is an explanation which the learned professor of constitutional law can give us later on, but I hope it will be good.
Previously, it was clear that orders in council could be passed only in pursuance of a

May 25, 1967

power conferred by or under the authority of an act. That is our understanding; that is the practice; that is the tradition; that is the way things must be. But we now seem to have added the right for a regulation or order in council to be made simply by or under the authority of the Governor in Council. I do not wish to dwell on this for long, but I must confess to the same anxiety and apprehension expressed by the hon. member for Peace River that this seems to be giving the Governor in Council a blank cheque in the matter of orders in council.
There is no doubt there have been times when governments have passed orders in council that have had doubtful validity. I can be quite impartial about this and refer to two recent examples, one under a Conservative government and one under a Liberal government. In the case of the Conservative government, I have in mind the import control order which was passed just after the election of June, 1962. The government of that day contended it had the right to do it on the basis of two statutes. Here in parliament we doubted that right. In due course certain people went to court over the matter. As a result of that the new government that came in after the next election decided that maybe there was some doubt and that that doubt should be taken care of by the passing of a new statute. At the moment I am not stating an opinion concerning who was right or who was wrong. I stated at the time what was-and still is- my view, but the point I am making is that it can happen that a government, even under the rules and regulations we now have, can enact an order in council of doubtful validity. What can parliament do, unless someone goes to court about it? Under the authority the executive has under our constitution, unless it is beaten on the floor of parliament, things which are quite illegal nevertheless have a way of standing.
I am thoroughly convinced that the order in council which the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) obtained from his colleagues with regard to the occupational retraining measure was invalid. It was in effect for a reasonably short period, from April 1 until May 8, or some time shortly thereafter. I suppose now that it has been confirmed by legislation there is no possibility of its ever being tested. Some of us will remain of the opinion that for a period of five or six weeks the government operated under an order in council which did not have constitutional validity. But, what can parliament or
Interpretation Act
the country do about it? The money has been spent under the provisions of this order in council. If a year or two from now the Auditor General finds that this should not have been done, all that will happen is that he will say in his report that this money was spent without proper authority. No one will go to jail for having broken the law. No law will be unscrambled; it was done by executive action and there it stands.
I cite these examples for the purpose of underlining the case made so effectively by the hon. member for Peace River; namely, that because errors can be made and because liberties can be taken with the right to pass orders in council, we should circumscribe those rights as carefully as we can to make sure that we are not placing in a statute of parliament words which give the government a blank cheque.
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) when he replies can satisfy us on the point I will be the first to admit he has made his case, if he makes it. However, I join with the hon. member for Peace River and other members of the house in saying that a very good case must be made, because I do not like to see parliament pass an act which says that the Governor in Council can pass an order in council simply by or under the authority of the Governor in Council.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
This is like lifting oneself up by one's bootstraps. It is like saying I have the authority because I have the authority. This should be looked into very carefully.
There is one other point I should like to make, but similar to many of one's points, it has subpoints. The explanatory note in this bill says that its purpose is to establish uniform definitions and modes of expression in order to eliminate repetition in our statutes and to facilitate the drafting and the construction of them. Let me cite a couple of examples which strike me as indicating that this desire for uniformity of definition has not been achieved.
There is a clause in the bill now before us to which I should like to make a passing reference before Your Honour feels he should remind us about references to clauses on second reading. This clause, which indicates how a person's age is to be determined, reads in such a manner that on the day of one's eighteenth birthday he becomes 18 years of age at the beginning of that day. If you look at the Criminal Code you will find a definition there which differs. It states that

May 25, 1967
Interpretation Act
you are not 18 years of age when the day of your eighteenth birthday arrives, but only when that day is fully completed.
Do not ask me what turns on this differ-*ence, but I find it passing strange that we should have a definition in the Criminal Code saying when you reach a certain age and a definition in the Interpretation Act which varies from that, even by just one day, especially when we are told that the purpose of this legislation is to establish uniform definitions.
I also noticed another clause in the bill now before us, specifically subclause (17) of clause 28, which defines "holiday". It lists a certain number of days as holidays. I would assume that if these days listed in the Interpretation Act as our holidays they should be the days which are holidays in this country. If you look at the Canada Labor (Standards) Code you will find a slight variation, and if your turn up the rules of the House of Commons you will find a day mentioned there that is not mentioned in either of these statutes. There are also questions arising about holidays that fall on Saturday and Sunday, and so on. I put these under the general heading of the contention that the purpose of this legislation is to provide uniformity. I have cited two examples where there is a lack of uniformity, and I should be glad to hear some explanation of this situation.
As I indicated, there seems to be no need for extensive discussion of this measure before us, but when we have one in respect of which we are told its purpose is simply to tidy things up, it always seems necessary to take a close look at it. Like the hon. gentleman who preceded me, I am particularly anxious to hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) about what seems to us to be a elause in the bill which would extend the powers of the government in respect of making orders in council. This is something about which we cannot but be concerned.

The contents of this particular bill go far beyond what was the initial intention of establishing uniform definitions and modes of expression, and the elimination of repetition in the statutes. The minister has a very heavy onus upon him tonight to establish that there is not being brought in by the back door some method or technique of restoring a prerogative right long since disappeared. I intend to sit down in time to give him plenty of opportunity to try to explain or answer these questions. supposedly dependant upon it, are going to be in fact presented. If the revised statutes for

The revised Statutes of Canada, 1967, should be published in 1967 rather than in

Mr. Speaker, there are two points with which I should like to deal. I shall first deal with the second point of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because it is the minor one. I think I can give an explanation in less than two minutes and then I will deal at greater length with the other point which was originally raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was concerned about the lack of uniformity of definitions. Of course he is quite right in pointing out that various statutes do have different definitions. The object of an interpretation act is precisely to tend toward uniformity of definition, but of course the interpretation act by itself is not essentially substantive law and cannot pretend to amend other acts such as the Criminal Code or the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, which were the two examples mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. We are discussing here an interpretation act which tends to give general definitions which will be applicable to the greatest possible number of statutes. In due course when we revise the other statutes, when they are before the house, I expect parliament will take into consideration the kind of remark that was made by the hon. member and achieve the laudable aim of reaching uniformity of definition. But of course we cannot do it by way of an interpretation act. All we are doing by way of the Interpretation Act is trying to get as large
Interpretation Act
a definition as possible applicable to the greatest number of acts.
There will always be, for particular statutes, particular definitions. It is not the intention of this bill, nor could it be the will of parliament, I think, to dispense in the future with all interpretive sections which appear at the beginning of each statute and which mean to give particular definitions to particular statutes.
This is a general one. Indeed, I hope that when we look at the various other statutes we will tend toward a general definition but we cannot, I repeat, do it by this Interpretation Act.
On the major point that was raised by the hon. member for Peace River and then taken up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), I appreciate and respect their point of view. In the few minutes that are left I will try to deal with it. I would make two points for the consideration of these hon. members. The first is that an interpretation act does not essentially, fundamentally, tend toward creating new powers and new rights for anybody.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: But it may.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It would, if parliament
spelled out quite precisely in an interpretation act or any other act that it was conferring new powers. But obviously if we read clause 2 (e) it is not conferring new powers to anyone; it is just giving a definition to the word "regulation". Clause 2 (e) says what the word "regulation" will mean in all other statutes and indeed in orders in council whether under the authority of an act or not. It is just saying what the word "regulation" will mean; it is giving no one the power to make regulations. That is the first point.
If this clause is read carefully I submit that it can in no sense be thought to be giving power to anyone. It is only giving a definition. The subtle argument which was brought forth by the hon. member for Peace River is that if this is so, if we are not giving any new powers, are we implying by clause 2 (e) (ii) that there is such a thing as a regulation made by governor in council not under the authority of an act? The answer of course is yes. The hon. member himself gave the reason for that. It is that the governor in council has inherited a certain number of prerogatives which are, I think, disappearing over-

May 25, 1967
Interpretation Act
the years as statutes come to indicate precisely what the prerogatives are. The prerogatives themselves may be replaced by a statute. But the hon. member very correctly referred to section 12 of the British North America Act and read it to mean that the governor in council could indeed exercise a certain number of prerogatives or authorities to make regulations, but regulations in the meaning of rule of court, by-law, commission, warrant or proclamation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not like to interrupt the minister but I wonder whether he would permit a question. If that is so, would it not be the case that although it might be invoking prerogatives which existed in England and in the provinces prior to 1867, nevertheless the governor in council was now purporting to act under section 12 of the British North America Act, which is a statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: I was coming to that point.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: I just did not want you to forget it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION, AND CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT OF OTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That is a very crucial point and I was precisely leading up to it. I am sure that the hon. member, by the way in which he has just stated his case, would not want to destroy all prerogative rights of the governor in council. There may be some which subsist. All the hon. member wants to point out is that if any do subsist, they come under an act, the British North America Act. I think I can convince him that his fear is not well founded if he reads the Interpretation Act. Section 2(l)(a) of the Interpretation Act provides that "act", means an act of the parliament of Canada. Therefore in clause 2 (e) (ii), when we talk about the execution of a power under the authority of an act, we can only mean under the authority of an act as defined by this act. "Act" means an act of the parliament of Canada. Therefore, if we did not have the second subparagraph and left only the first, we would be destroying any authority given to the word "regulation" in its broad sense under section 12 of the British North America Act, which is not an act of the parliament of Canada.
I must remind hon. members that the Interpretation Act itself has an interpretation section, which is the section we are now discussing. This interpretation section specifies the act we are now discussing, which is an act of the parliament of Canada and not an act of the United Kingdom parliament, as is the
fMr. Trudeau.]
British North America Act. Therefore on these grounds I would suggest to the hon. member that unless he wants to destroy all prerogatives which might belong to the governor in council he should not press the type of amendment he was suggesting.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I would say that I share completely the concern of these hon. members for restraining as much as possible the authority of any government to act through order in council not under the authority of a statute. I think that in the last analysis parliament must confer the overwhelming majority of any authority which can be exercised by the governor in council and therefore it must be conferred by statute. But I am suggesting to these hon. members that we should not, by way of an interpretation statute, presume to destroy the whole idea of prerogatives which might belong to the governor in council. Perhaps we would want to envisage that and these hon. members would want to submit a statute to that effect.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
But I am suggesting that the Interpretation Act is not the place to do this because, once again, it does not tend to confer new powers or to destroy old ones. It merely tends to give the legislators, the judges and the citizens who are reading the acts, the rules and definitions which permit the statutes and the regulations to be as simple as possible, not cluttered up with endless interpretation sections at the beginning of the statutes.
